```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(gt)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 18))
sex_cols <- c(Male = "#0072B2", Female = "#D55E00")

# number formatting helpers for inline results
f  <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(unname(x), format = "f", digits = d)
fp <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste("=", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))

# vectorised formatters and a common table style for the output slides
fnum <- function(x, d = 2) ifelse(is.na(x), "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
fpv  <- function(p) ifelse(is.na(p), "", ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3)))

nice_table <- function(df, title = NULL, highlight = NULL) {
  tab <- gt(df) |>
    tab_options(table.font.size = px(22),
                heading.title.font.size = px(24),
                column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
                table.width = pct(100))
  if (!is.null(title)) tab <- tab_header(tab, title = title)
  if (!is.null(highlight)) {
    tab <- tab_style(tab, style = cell_fill(color = "#FFF3CD"),
                     locations = cells_body(rows = highlight))
  }
  tab
}

# ---- Lizard data (Verbeke) ----
raw   <- readLines("data/lizard.sas")
start <- grep("^cards;", raw) + 1
end   <- grep("^;", raw)[1] - 1
lizard <- read.table(text = raw[start:end],
                     col.names = c("moth", "sex", "dors"),
                     na.strings = ".") |>
  filter(!is.na(dors)) |>
  mutate(sex    = factor(sex, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Male", "Female")),
         mother = factor(moth)) |>
  group_by(mother) |>
  mutate(m_mean = mean(dors)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(mother_ord = reorder(mother, m_mean))

mother_means <- distinct(lizard, mother_ord, m_mean)

# t-test ignoring mothers
tt <- t.test(dors ~ sex, data = lizard, var.equal = TRUE)
diff_raw <- diff(tapply(lizard$dors, lizard$sex, mean))  # female - male

# mother as fixed effect
fit_fixed <- lm(dors ~ mother + sex, data = lizard)
p_fixed   <- anova(fit_fixed)["sex", "Pr(>F)"]

# linear mixed model
fit_lmm <- lmer(dors ~ sex + (1 | mother), data = lizard)
co  <- summary(fit_lmm)$coefficients
vc  <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_lmm))
s2m <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "mother"]
s2e <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"]
icc <- s2m / (s2m + s2e)

var_df <- data.frame(
  part  = factor(c("Between mothers", "Within mothers"),
                 levels = c("Within mothers", "Between mothers")),
  share = c(s2m, s2e) / (s2m + s2e)
)
var_df$lab <- paste0(var_df$part, ": ", round(100 * var_df$share), "%")

# predictions per mother and for the average mother
pred_grid <- expand.grid(mother = levels(lizard$mother),
                         sex    = levels(lizard$sex),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |>
  mutate(mother = factor(mother, levels = levels(lizard$mother)),
         sex    = factor(sex, levels = levels(lizard$sex)))
pred_grid$fit <- predict(fit_lmm, newdata = pred_grid)

pop_pred <- data.frame(sex = factor(levels(lizard$sex), levels = levels(lizard$sex)))
pop_pred$fit <- predict(fit_lmm, newdata = pop_pred, re.form = NA)

# ---- Simulated learning task (binary outcome) ----
set.seed(2026)
n_id     <- 30
sessions <- 1:8
n_trials <- 10
b_true   <- rnorm(n_id, mean = 0, sd = 1.5)

learn <- expand.grid(id = 1:n_id, session = sessions, trial = 1:n_trials)
learn$correct <- rbinom(nrow(learn), size = 1,
                        prob = plogis(-1.5 + 0.5 * (learn$session - 1) + b_true[learn$id]))
learn$id <- factor(learn$id)

learn_sum <- learn |>
  group_by(id, session) |>
  summarise(p = mean(correct), .groups = "drop")

fit_glmm  <- glmer(correct ~ session + (1 | id), family = binomial, data = learn)
beta_glmm <- fixef(fit_glmm)
sd_b      <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_glmm))$sdcor[1]

# individual, typical and population-average curves
s_grid <- seq(min(sessions), max(sessions), length.out = 100)
b_hat  <- ranef(fit_glmm)$id[[1]]
ind_curves <- expand.grid(session = s_grid, id = seq_along(b_hat))
ind_curves$p <- plogis(beta_glmm[1] + beta_glmm[2] * ind_curves$session + b_hat[ind_curves$id])

b_draw <- rnorm(5000, mean = 0, sd = sd_b)
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(session = s_grid,
             p = plogis(beta_glmm[1] + beta_glmm[2] * s_grid),
             type = "Typical individual (b = 0)"),
  data.frame(session = s_grid,
             p = sapply(s_grid, function(s) mean(plogis(beta_glmm[1] + beta_glmm[2] * s + b_draw))),
             type = "Population average")
)
```

::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.title data-id="title"}
Lightning Introduction to Generalized Linear Mixed Models
:::

Mauricio Moreno, PhD

![](images/sample_back.jpg){.image-left}


## Today's goals {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

::: {.incremental}
1. **Recognise** when your data are grouped (repeated trials, siblings, individuals in social groups) and why that breaks the independence assumption.
2. **Explain** what a random intercept is and what the intraclass correlation tells you.
3. **Choose** between a linear mixed model and a GLMM based on the type of your response.
4. **Interpret** the coefficients of a GLMM as effects for the *typical individual*.
:::

::: {.callout-note .fragment}
At the end, we turn these goals into three questions to ask about **your own data**.
:::

::::

## What is a linear model? {.smaller}

::: v-stack

Simply put, a linear model is a mathematical equation that predicts a continuous dependent variable ($y$) as a linear combination of one or more predictors ($x$):


$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \cdots + \beta_n X_n + \epsilon
$$

:::: {.columns .v-center .fragment}

::: {.column width="40%"}
Where:

- $\beta_0$: intercept
- $\beta_1, \dots, \beta_n$: effects of the predictors
- $\epsilon$: residual error, assumed $\epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$
:::

::: {.column width="60%" .fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## What does "linear" mean?

- Linear does **not** mean the relationship between $x$ and $y$ has to be a straight line. It means the model is **linear in the parameters** ($\beta$).
- Predictors can be transformed (e.g., $X^2$, $\log X$) and it is still a linear model, as long as each $\beta$ only multiplies a term and is added up:
  - $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_2 X^2 + \epsilon$ ✅ linear (a curve!)
  - $y = \beta_0 \, e^{\beta_1 X} + \epsilon$ ❌ not linear, because $\beta_1$ sits inside the exponential
:::
:::

::::

:::

## One model, many names {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

Many methods you already know are special cases of the linear model:

::: {.incremental}
- **Simple and multiple linear regression:** predicts a continuous $y$ from one or more predictors.
- **t-test:** compares two group means (one binary predictor).
- **ANOVA:** compares two or more group means using categorical predictors.
- **ANCOVA:** combines categorical and continuous predictors to compare group means, adjusting for a covariate.
- **Generalized linear models (GLM):** extend the idea to other types of responses, such as binary (logistic regression) or counts (Poisson regression), by linking the mean of $y$ to the predictors through a **link function**.
:::

::: {.callout-important .fragment}
All of them assume that **observations are independent**. What happens when they are not?
:::

::::



## A simple question {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

::::: {.columns .v-center}

::: {.column width="45%"}
**102 lizards.** Do males and females differ in the number of **dorsal scales**?

::: {.fragment}
A two-sample t-test (or `lm(dors ~ sex)`):

- Females minus males: `r f(diff_raw)` scales
- $p$ `r fp(tt$p.value)`
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
Conclusion: **no evidence** of a sex difference... right?
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: plot-sex
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(lizard, aes(sex, dors, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.3, outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = sex), width = 0.12, height = 0.15,
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Dorsal scales") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
:::

:::::

::::

## Full output: t-test {.smaller}

```r
t.test(dors ~ sex, data = lizard, var.equal = TRUE)
```

::::: {.columns .v-center}

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Mean (males)", "Mean (females)", "Difference (males - females)",
                "95% CI of the difference", "t", "df", "p-value"),
  Value = c(fnum(tt$estimate[1]), fnum(tt$estimate[2]),
            fnum(tt$estimate[1] - tt$estimate[2]),
            paste0("[", fnum(tt$conf.int[1]), ", ", fnum(tt$conf.int[2]), "]"),
            fnum(tt$statistic), fnum(tt$parameter, 0), fpv(tt$p.value))
) |>
  nice_table(title = "Two-sample t-test", highlight = c(6, 7))
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}
**Where to look:**

- **p-value**: the one on the previous slide
- **df = `r fnum(tt$parameter, 0)`**: R treats all 102 lizards as **independent** observations
:::

:::::

## But wait... who are their mothers? {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

The 102 lizards come from **`r nlevels(lizard$mother)` mothers**.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mothers
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 3.6
ggplot(lizard, aes(mother_ord, dors, colour = sex)) +
  geom_errorbar(data = mother_means,
                aes(x = mother_ord, ymin = m_mean, ymax = m_mean),
                inherit.aes = FALSE, width = 0.7,
                colour = "grey55", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0.1, seed = 1),
             size = 2.8, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sex_cols, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Mother (ordered by average number of scales)",
       y = "Dorsal scales") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "top")
```

::: {.incremental}
- Lots of variability **between** mothers (grey bars = mother averages).
- **Within** a mother, males tend to have more scales.
- Siblings are more alike than unrelated lizards: observations are **not independent**.
:::

::::

## Hierarchical data {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

::::: {.callout-fit}
::: {.callout-tip}
*"Hierarchical data are obtained when the sample is taken at multiple, hierarchically ordered, levels."*^[Verbeke, G. (2013). *Concepts of multilevel, longitudinal, and mixed models*. Lecture notes, KU Leuven.]
:::
:::::

::::: {.columns .v-center}

::: {.column width="55%" .fragment}
**Our lizards:**

- Level 2: `r nlevels(lizard$mother)` **mothers**
  - Level 1: 102 **lizards** (sex measured on each lizard)

**In CBB research, for example:**

- Social groups → individuals → trials
:::

::: {.column width="45%" .fragment}
Also known as:

- Repeated measures
- Longitudinal data
- Multilevel data
- **[Clustered or correlated data]{.danger}**
:::

:::::

::::: {.callout-fit .fragment}
::: {.callout-important}
Hierarchical data are usually **not independent**. The key question is: how do we **account for the association** between observations from the same cluster?
:::
:::::

::::

## Option 1: mother as a fixed effect? {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

```r
lm(dors ~ mother + sex, data = lizard)
```

::: {.incremental}
- It works: the sex effect is now significant ($p$ `r fp(p_fixed)`).
- But it spends **`r nlevels(lizard$mother) - 1` parameters** just on the mothers.
- And we are not interested in *these* `r nlevels(lizard$mother)` mothers, but in lizard mothers **in general**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .fragment}
## Idea
Treat the mothers as a **random sample** from a population of mothers, and estimate how much they **vary**.
:::

::::

## Full output: mother as a fixed effect {.smaller}

```r
fit_fixed <- lm(dors ~ mother + sex, data = lizard)
anova(fit_fixed)
```

::::: {.columns .v-center}

::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
a_tab <- anova(fit_fixed)
data.frame(
  Term      = rownames(a_tab),
  Df        = fnum(a_tab$Df, 0),
  `Sum Sq`  = fnum(a_tab$`Sum Sq`),
  `Mean Sq` = fnum(a_tab$`Mean Sq`),
  F         = fnum(a_tab$`F value`),
  `p-value` = fpv(a_tab$`Pr(>F)`),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  nice_table(title = "ANOVA table", highlight = c(1, 2))
```
:::

::: {.column width="38%" .fragment}
**Where to look:**

- Row **sex**: the sex effect, tested **after** adjusting for mother
- Row **mother**: **Df = `r fnum(a_tab$Df[1], 0)`**, the parameters spent on the mothers
:::

:::::

## The linear mixed model {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

::::: {.columns .v-center}

::: {.column width="50%"}
$$
y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \alpha_i + \beta_1 \, \text{sex}_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij}
$$

$$
\alpha_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{mother}), \qquad \epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

- $i$: mother, $j$: lizard within mother
- $\alpha_i$: **random intercept**, each mother has her own baseline

::: {.fragment}
```r
library(lmerTest)
lmer(dors ~ sex + (1 | mother), data = lizard)
```

Sex effect: `r f(co["sexFemale", "Estimate"])` scales (SE `r f(co["sexFemale", "Std. Error"])`), $p$ `r fp(co["sexFemale", "Pr(>|t|)"])`
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
```{r}
#| label: plot-ranint
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(pred_grid, aes(sex, fit, group = mother)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey70", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = pop_pred, aes(group = 1), colour = "black", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(data = pop_pred, aes(group = 1, colour = sex), size = 5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Predicted dorsal scales",
       subtitle = "Grey: each mother   Black: average mother") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
:::

:::::

::::

## Full output: linear mixed model {.smaller}

```r
fit_lmm <- lmer(dors ~ sex + (1 | mother), data = lizard)
summary(fit_lmm)
```

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
data.frame(
  Term      = rownames(co),
  Estimate  = fnum(co[, "Estimate"]),
  SE        = fnum(co[, "Std. Error"]),
  df        = fnum(co[, "df"], 1),
  t         = fnum(co[, "t value"]),
  `p-value` = fpv(co[, "Pr(>|t|)"]),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  nice_table(title = "Fixed effects", highlight = 2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
```{r}
data.frame(
  Group      = vc$grp,
  Variance   = fnum(vc$vcov),
  `Std. Dev.` = fnum(vc$sdcor),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  nice_table(title = "Random effects", highlight = c(1, 2))
```
:::

:::::

`r nobs(fit_lmm)` observations, `r ngrps(fit_lmm)` mothers: R now knows the data are **grouped**.

::: {.fragment}
**Where to look:** the **variances** are the numbers behind the ICC; row **sexFemale** is the difference between females and males.
:::

## How alike are siblings? {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

The model splits the total variability into two parts:

$$
\underbrace{`r f(s2m + s2e)`}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{`r f(s2m)`}_{\sigma^2_{mother}} + \underbrace{`r f(s2e)`}_{\sigma^2}
$$

```{r}
#| label: plot-icc
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 1.6
#| fig-align: "center"
ggplot(var_df, aes(x = 1, y = share, fill = part)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = lab), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            colour = "white", size = 6, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Between mothers" = "#0072B2",
                               "Within mothers" = "#999999")) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.fragment}
**Intraclass correlation (ICC):** $\rho = \frac{\sigma^2_{mother}}{\sigma^2_{mother} + \sigma^2} = `r f(icc)`$

Two lizards from the same mother are correlated with $\rho \approx$ `r f(icc)`. The larger the ICC, the more it matters to account for the grouping.
:::

::::

## What if $y$ is not continuous? {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

Remember $\epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$? It breaks down for many outcomes in CBB research:

::: {.incremental}
- **Binary:** chose the correct option, looked at the target (0/1)
- **Counts:** number of vocalisations, spikes, aggressive interactions
:::

::::: {.columns .v-center .fragment}

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Example (simulated):** `r n_id` individuals do a learning task, `r n_trials` trials per session over `r length(sessions)` sessions. Outcome: correct (1) or not (0).

Like a GLM, we model the **log-odds** through a **link function**:

$$
\text{logit}(\pi) = \log\frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}
$$
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: plot-learn
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.8
ggplot(learn_sum, aes(session, p)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = id), colour = "grey70", alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 2, colour = "#D55E00") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sessions) +
  labs(x = "Session", y = "Proportion correct",
       subtitle = "Grey: each individual   Orange: average")
```
:::

:::::

::::

## The generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

$$
\text{correct}_{ij} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}), \qquad
\text{logit}(\pi_{ij}) = \beta_0 + b_i + \beta_1 \, \text{session}_{ij}, \qquad
b_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_b)
$$

::: {.fragment}
```r
glmer(correct ~ session + (1 | id), family = binomial, data = learn)
```
:::

::: {.incremental}
- $\hat\beta_1 =$ `r f(beta_glmm["session"])`: for a **typical individual**, the odds of a correct answer are multiplied by **`r f(exp(beta_glmm["session"]))`** per session.
- $\hat\sigma_b =$ `r f(sd_b)`: individuals differ a lot in their baseline performance.
- Same logic as before: the random effect $b_i$ accounts for repeated trials from the same individual.
:::

::::

## Full output: GLMM {.smaller}

```r
fit_glmm <- glmer(correct ~ session + (1 | id), family = binomial, data = learn)
summary(fit_glmm)
```

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
cg <- summary(fit_glmm)$coefficients
data.frame(
  Term         = rownames(cg),
  Estimate     = fnum(cg[, "Estimate"]),
  SE           = fnum(cg[, "Std. Error"]),
  z            = fnum(cg[, "z value"]),
  `p-value`    = fpv(cg[, "Pr(>|z|)"]),
  `Odds ratio` = fnum(exp(cg[, "Estimate"])),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  nice_table(title = "Fixed effects (log-odds scale)", highlight = 2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
```{r}
vcg <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_glmm))
data.frame(
  Group       = vcg$grp,
  Variance    = fnum(vcg$vcov),
  `Std. Dev.` = fnum(vcg$sdcor),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  nice_table(title = "Random effects", highlight = 1)
```
:::

:::::

::: {.fragment}
**Where to look:**

- Row **session**: change in **log-odds** per session for a typical individual; the **odds ratio** is `exp()` of it
- **Std. Dev.** of `id`: how much individuals differ. There is no Residual row: for binary data, that variability comes from the Bernoulli distribution
:::

## One thing to remember {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

::::: {.columns .v-center}

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: plot-marginal
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = ind_curves, aes(session, p, group = id),
            colour = "grey80") +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(session, p, colour = type, linetype = type),
            linewidth = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Typical individual (b = 0)" = "#0072B2",
                                 "Population average" = "#D55E00"),
                      name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Typical individual (b = 0)" = "solid",
                                   "Population average" = "dashed"),
                        name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Session", y = "P(correct)") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "vertical")
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Grey: predicted curve for each individual.
- **Average curve ≠ curve of the average individual.**
- In a GLMM, the coefficients describe the **typical individual**, not the population average.
:::

::: {.callout-important .fragment}
In a linear mixed model the two coincide. With a link function (logit, log), they do not.
:::
:::

:::::

::::

## Before you fit a mixed model, ask... {.smaller}

:::: v-stack

::: {.incremental}
1. **What are my units, and how are they grouped?** (trials in individuals, individuals in groups, ...)
2. **What type is my response?** Continuous, binary, count: this chooses the family and link.
3. **Is my question about the typical individual or the population?**
:::

::::: {.callout-fit .fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
